result: The authors developed Ais, an open-source cryoET segmentation software package with comprehensive annotation, training, segmentation, and rendering functionality. The software includes a library of neural network architectures, supports interactive segmentation at fast framerates, and can run on relatively low-end GPUs. It is available on GitHub and Python package index, with documentation and tutorials provided.
evaluation: Claims C4-C170 collectively describe the software's features, capabilities, and availability. The software is demonstrated through figures showing the interface, workflow, and outputs. The technical specifications (file formats, hardware requirements, dependencies) are clearly stated, and availability is documented with specific URLs and repositories.

result: An open model repository was established at aiscryoet.org where users can upload and download trained models, with 27 models from the manuscript uploaded to kickstart the repository. This allows users to skip annotation and training steps.
evaluation: Claims C38-C41 and C142 describe the model repository with specific details about its function and initial content. Figure 1D-E shows the repository interface. The availability of 27 models is a verifiable factual claim, and the purpose of enabling model sharing is clearly demonstrated.

result: Six neural network architectures were compared for segmenting three features (membranes, carbon, antibody platforms) in IgG3 liposome datasets. VGGNet performed best for membranes while UNet performed best for carbon and antibody platforms based on loss values, but Pix2pix generated better segmentations for antibody platforms despite worse loss values, demonstrating that loss values don't fully capture model performance.
evaluation: Claims C49-C62 describe a systematic comparison experiment with results presented in Table 1 and Figure 2. The methodology is detailed in C145-C148. The key finding that loss values don't correlate perfectly with human-judged quality (C54-C56) is demonstrated visually in Figure 2C. The conclusion that no single architecture is universally best (C59) is well-supported by the data.

result: A system of proximity-based 'model interactions' (colocalization and avoidance) and 'model competition' was implemented to reduce false positive segmentations by conditionally combining predictions from multiple neural networks. This approach successfully suppressed common erroneous segmentations, though sometimes at the expense of increased false negatives.
evaluation: Claims C66-C83 describe the model interaction system with technical implementation details (C69-C78) and demonstrate its effectiveness through specific examples (C80-C81). Figure 3 shows the interface (3A), specific examples of interaction effects (3B-C), and a systematic comparison (3D) demonstrating reduction in false positives. The trade-off with false negatives (C83) is acknowledged.

result: Ais successfully automated particle picking for subtomogram averaging of IgG3 antibody platforms and antibody-C1 complexes, reducing manual picking time from ~20 hours to ~1 hour for annotation. The automated approach yielded 2499 antibody platform particles and 602 antibody-C1 complex particles, producing reconstructions highly similar to those from manual picking.
evaluation: Claims C91-C115 describe a complete particle picking experiment with clear methodology (C96-C109), quantitative results (C112), and validation (C114). Figure 4 shows the complete workflow from annotation to final reconstructions. Figure 4—figure supplement 3 provides FSC curves demonstrating that automated picking achieved the same 44 Å resolution as the original manual picking. The dramatic time savings (C95, C98) are documented.

result: Ais successfully segmented seven distinct features in C. reinhardtii cilia (membranes, ribosomes, microtubule doublets, axial microtubules, non-microtubular filaments, IFTs, and glycocalyx) from a complex dataset with >20 identifiable features. The segmentation correctly identified key biological structures including the ribosome exclusion zone.
evaluation: Claims C120-C127 describe segmentation of a complex cellular dataset with results shown in Figure 5A. The biological accuracy is validated by correctly identifying the ribosome exclusion zone (C125), a known feature from the original publication. The challenge of the dataset (C122-C123) and quality of results (C124-C127) are clearly documented.

result: Ais successfully segmented six features in mouse neuron mitochondria, including distinguishing between vesicular membranes and mitochondrial cristae membranes, as well as identifying mitochondrial granules, microtubules, actin filaments, and ribosomes.
evaluation: Claims C128-C130 describe segmentation of mitochondrial features with results shown in Figure 5B. The ability to distinguish between highly similar membrane types (vesicular vs. cristae) demonstrates the software's discriminatory power. The dataset source (Wu et al., 2023, EMDB-29207) is properly cited.

result: Ais generated 3D visualizations of ten distinct cellular features in coronavirus-infected cells, including distinguishing between single and double membranes, discriminating between cytoskeletal filaments, and identifying viral components (nucleocapsid proteins, pores, nucleic acids). Processing took ~3 minutes per feature after training, and models can be applied to other volumes without retraining.
evaluation: Claims C131-C139 describe the most complex segmentation demonstration with ten features shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1. The ability to distinguish similar structures (C132-C133) and identify specific viral components (C134-C136) is visually demonstrated. Processing time (C138) and model reusability (C139) are documented, though the 'some hours' for annotation (C137) is imprecise.

result: The manuscript establishes the importance of segmentation in cryoET workflows and identifies challenges in automated segmentation, particularly for complex cellular datasets where structures are visually similar or difficult to isolate.
evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C10-C11, C84-C90, and C116-C119 provide established knowledge about cryoET segmentation workflows and challenges. These are well-accepted facts in the field and provide context for the software development. The specific challenges mentioned (C89-C90, C118-C119) motivate the technical solutions presented.

result: The authors identified a gap in available cryoET segmentation software, noting that existing tools have limitations in scope, accessibility, or open availability, with some popular programs not being free to use.
evaluation: Claims C3, C12, C14-C15 represent the authors' assessment of existing software limitations. While C13 (Amira not being free) is verifiable, the broader claims about limitations of other software (C14) and the existence of a 'deficit' (C15) are subjective assessments. The comparison with other tools (C42-C45) acknowledges that similar functionality exists elsewhere, which somewhat contradicts the claim of a clear deficit.

result: The authors suggest that cryoET datasets, especially cellular samples, look similar enough that models trained on one dataset might work on another with different pixel sizes.
evaluation: Claim C36 is a general observation, while C37 is explicitly labeled as speculation in the evidence. The model repository (C38-C41) is built on this premise, but the manuscript doesn't provide systematic validation of cross-dataset model transferability. This remains a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated result.

result: Existing software packages (EMAN2, MIB, SuRVOS, QuPath) provide some or most of the functionality available in Ais.
evaluation: Claim C42-C45 acknowledge prior work with proper citations. This is a fair assessment of the software landscape and demonstrates that the authors are aware of existing tools. However, no detailed comparison of capabilities is provided.

result: The authors recommend increasing validation split size when training datasets are large and note that more powerful GPUs are useful for batch processing.
evaluation: Claims C151 and C159 are practical recommendations based on the authors' experience. These are reasonable suggestions supported by standard machine learning practice, though they are not experimentally validated in the manuscript.

result: Data collection and processing for the antibody experiments followed established protocols from a previous publication, using standard cryoET instrumentation and reconstruction software.
evaluation: Claims C160-C164 describe methodology with proper citations to previous work (Abendstein et al., 2023) and standard software packages (IMOD, EMAN, Dynamo). These are factual statements about methods used, properly documented with citations.

result: The neural network comparison experiments (Table 1) were performed using an NVIDIA Quadro P2200 GPU on a PC with an Intel i9-10900K CPU.
evaluation: Claim C156 provides specific hardware information for reproducibility. This is a factual statement about the experimental setup.
